appendectomy.name: Appendicectomy
appendectomy.what: Removal of the inflamed appendix, the blind-ended tube hanging off the caecum at the start of the large intestine. Usually done through three small keyhole incisions with a camera (laparoscopically), occasionally through a single cut in the right lower abdomen. The appendix usually needs to come out as soon as appendicitis is diagnosed, because an inflamed appendix can burst and spread infection through the lining of the abdomen (peritonitis), which can be life-threatening. Keyhole surgery is the usual first choice when appendicitis is found early; if the surgeon meets difficulties or judges it safer, the operation is converted to an open approach, which is regarded as sound surgical judgement rather than a failure. With enhanced-recovery care many people with uncomplicated appendicitis go home within a day.
why: Acute appendicitis, to prevent perforation and peritonitis; surgeons usually recommend removal even when antibiotics have settled an episode, because a proportion of people treated with antibiotics alone have another attack
An appendix mass or abscess after initial antibiotics and drainage, with the operation deferred until the inflammation has settled
Occasionally, an appendix tumour found on imaging or during other surgery
before: Blood tests, pregnancy test in women, sometimes ultrasound or CT. The diagnosis is mainly clinical; blood tests show inflammation and imaging is used when the picture is unclear
Nil by mouth; intravenous fluids and antibiotics
If an abscess has already formed, surgery is often postponed: antibiotics are given and the abscess may be drained through a small cut in the skin, with the appendix removed later
Consent and marking; general anaesthetic. Previous abdominal surgery is noted because scar tissue raises the chance of injury when the keyhole instruments are inserted
steps: Carbon dioxide inflates the abdomen through a port at the navel to create working space
A camera and two instruments are introduced through 5-12 mm ports
The appendix is lifted, its blood supply in the mesoappendix sealed, and its base tied or stapled at the caecum
The appendix is removed in a bag; any pus is washed out
If inflammation, scarring or bleeding makes the keyhole view unsafe, the surgeon converts to an open incision in the right lower abdomen
Ports are removed and the small wounds closed with dissolvable stitches
after: Home the same or next day for uncomplicated cases; a few days in hospital after open surgery, a perforated appendix or complications
Simple painkillers; walk early. Getting out of bed the day after surgery lowers the risk of blood clots in the legs and eases muscle soreness

Pain and bruising around the wounds for the first few days, and shoulder-tip pain for up to a week from the gas used to inflate the abdomen, are expected; constipation or diarrhoea for a few days is common
Antibiotics continued for a few days if the appendix had perforated
appendectomy.recovery: Back to desk work in about a week and to sport in two to four weeks after keyhole surgery; longer after open surgery or a perforated appendix. Most people recover from keyhole surgery within a couple of weeks, although studies of convalescence suggest full recovery often takes around two weeks on average and is slower when there were complications. After open surgery strenuous activity is avoided for several weeks. Pain and indigestion are the commonest complaints in the first days and settle as the bowel recovers.
risks: Wound infection (more after perforation)
Pelvic abscess, or an abscess where the appendix was removed
Bleeding, injury to bowel, bladder or blood vessels during instrument insertion (uncommon; more likely after previous abdominal surgery)
Stump leak, adhesions (scar tissue inside the abdomen, which can rarely cause a bowel blockage years later), hernia at the port site (rare)
Anaesthetic risks
All risks are higher when the appendix has already burst; peritonitis from a burst appendix can be life-threatening and needs urgent surgery and antibiotics
alternatives: Antibiotics alone for uncomplicated appendicitis: a course of tablets at home, or intravenous antibiotics in hospital for severe cases. It works in most people in the short term, but a proportion have another episode and about a third need surgery within a few years, so surgeons usually still recommend removal
Drainage and delayed surgery for an abscess

cholecystectomy.name: Cholecystectomy
cholecystectomy.what: Removal of the gallbladder, the small sac under the liver that stores bile. The commonest planned abdominal operation, almost always done by keyhole surgery. The liver keeps making bile, which then flows straight into the duodenum. Surgery is the usual treatment for gallstones because, once stones have caused symptoms, they tend to do so again; gallstones that cause no symptoms generally need no treatment, although symptoms may appear later. The operation is done under general anaesthetic and usually takes one to two hours. Compared with the open operation, the keyhole approach means smaller wounds, less pain, a shorter hospital stay, a faster return to work and fewer wound infections. An open cholecystectomy is chosen when the gallbladder is severely inflamed, infected or scarred from previous operations, and the surgeon may switch to open surgery if problems arise during a keyhole procedure. The gallbladder is not an essential organ and people live normally without it, though bile then enters the gut continuously rather than in response to meals.
why: Gallstones causing repeated pain (biliary colic)
Acute cholecystitis (an inflamed, infected gallbladder)
Gallstone pancreatitis, once recovered, to prevent recurrence
Gallbladder polyps above 10 mm or a porcelain gallbladder (cancer risk)
A gallbladder that does not empty properly (biliary dyskinesia) causing typical pain without stones, in selected cases
before: Ultrasound confirming stones; liver function tests; MRCP or ERCP if stones are suspected in the bile duct. Deranged liver tests or a dilated duct raise the suspicion of duct stones, which are cleared endoscopically before or around the time of surgery
Fasting; general anaesthetic
Antibiotics at induction if inflamed
Explanation of the operation, the possibility of conversion to open surgery and the risk of bile duct injury, and consent
steps: Four ports: one at the navel for the camera, three under the right ribs; carbon dioxide inflates the abdomen to create working space
The gallbladder is retracted upward to expose Calot's triangle
The cystic duct and cystic artery are identified with a 'critical view of safety', clipped and divided

The gallbladder is peeled off the liver bed with diathermy and removed in a bag through the navel port; the bag prevents stones spilling into the abdomen, where they can cause abscesses long afterwards
An X-ray of the bile duct (cholangiogram) may be done during the operation
If the anatomy cannot be seen safely because of inflammation, scarring or bleeding, the operation is converted to an open incision under the right ribs
after: Home the same day or next morning
Shoulder-tip pain from residual gas for a day or two; some pain or discomfort at the wounds for a few days
Wounds are kept clean and dry; showering is usually allowed after a couple of days, with baths and swimming delayed until the wounds have healed
Normal diet resumed; some people notice looser stools after fatty meals

Worsening pain, fever, redness or discharge from a wound, persistent vomiting or yellowing of the skin or eyes are reported promptly, because they can indicate infection, a bile leak or a retained duct stone
cholecystectomy.recovery: Most people return to normal activities within two weeks; heavy lifting avoided for a few weeks. After an uncomplicated keyhole operation many people are back to normal physical activity in about a week, while recovery from open surgery takes longer. Digestion adjusts to the continuous flow of bile; a minority have ongoing loose stools or intolerance of fatty food, and a small number develop persistent pain, bloating or diarrhoea (post-cholecystectomy syndrome) that needs further assessment.
risks: Bile leak from the liver bed or cystic duct stump (1-2%), which can cause bile peritonitis or an abscess and may need a drain or endoscopic stent
Injury to the common bile duct (about 1 in 300), the serious complication, which may need specialist reconstructive surgery
Bleeding, infection of a wound or inside the abdomen, retained stones in the duct, pancreatitis
Stones spilled during surgery, which rarely cause abscesses or pain months or years later
Conversion to open surgery (a few per cent, more in acute inflammation), which is a safety decision rather than a complication
General anaesthetic risks and blood clots in the legs or lungs
alternatives: Watchful waiting for stones with no symptoms, which usually need no treatment
Antibiotics and a drainage tube (cholecystostomy) in patients too unwell for surgery
Bile-acid tablets for tiny stones (slow, often recur); non-surgical treatments are only an option for cholesterol stones, not pigment stones

knee-replacement.name: Knee replacement
knee-replacement.what: The worn surfaces at the end of the femur and top of the tibia are cut away and capped with metal components, with a polyethylene insert between them as the new cartilage; the back of the kneecap is often resurfaced. A partial replacement treats one compartment only when the rest of the joint is healthy, through a smaller incision and usually with a quicker recovery. The operation is considered when arthritis pain is severe enough to limit walking and daily life and is no longer controlled by tablets, exercise and injections. It is a major operation: some blood loss is expected and a transfusion is occasionally needed, and the body's response to surgery and anaesthetic carries general risks to the heart, lungs and wound healing that are higher in smokers, in diabetes and when immunity is weakened. The implant is a mechanical device that wears over time; most last for many years, but younger and more active people are more likely to need a revision operation at some stage.
why: Severe osteoarthritis (or rheumatoid arthritis) with pain that limits walking, sleep and daily life despite painkillers, physiotherapy, weight loss and injections
Post-traumatic arthritis after fractures
Rarely, tumours or failed previous surgery
before: Standing X-rays; blood tests, ECG, MRSA screen, dental check
'Joint school' education, prehabilitation exercises, weight optimisation; stopping smoking and good diabetic control lower the risk of wound problems and infection
An explanation of the expected benefits, the risks and the alternatives, and consent; the operation is planned so that pain relief, early walking and clot prevention start on the day of surgery
Spinal or general anaesthetic with nerve blocks
steps: A vertical incision over the front of the knee; the kneecap is moved aside
Guided cuts remove a few millimetres from the end of the femur and top of the tibia, and worn cartilage and the cruciate ligaments as required
Trial components are fitted and the ligament balance and alignment checked through the full range of movement
The final metal components are cemented (or press-fitted) and the plastic insert locked in
The joint is washed, local anaesthetic infiltrated, and the layers closed
after: Standing and walking with a frame the same day or next; getting the knee moving early with the therapy team improves the final result
Physiotherapy from day one: bending, straightening, stairs; home in 1-3 days
Blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2-6 weeks; ice and elevation; compression stockings and early walking also reduce the risk of clots
Pain and stiffness in the first weeks are normal and are managed with regular painkillers; difficulty passing urine in the first day after a spinal anaesthetic is common and usually settles
Wound check at two weeks; six-week and one-year reviews

Urgent review is needed for a hot, red or increasingly painful knee, oozing or pus from the wound, a high temperature, or throbbing calf pain; chest pain or breathlessness is an emergency because it may indicate a clot in the lung
knee-replacement.recovery: Walking without aids by about six weeks, driving at 6-8 weeks, most of the benefit by three months and continued improvement for a year. A knee replacement usually lasts 15-25 years. Most people who follow their rehabilitation programme resume nearly all normal activities within about three to six weeks, and daily life improves for the great majority. A minority are left with lasting problems: limited bending, ongoing pain or stiffness, or a knee that feels unstable when standing or walking, for which further physiotherapy or occasionally another operation is considered.
risks: Deep infection (about 1%), the most serious, sometimes needing revision; superficial wound infections are treated with antibiotics, while deep infection can appear early or years later
Blood clots in the leg or lung, among the commonest serious complications despite prevention
Stiffness needing manipulation under anaesthetic or arthroscopy, the most frequent complication; scar tissue can limit bending
Loosening or wear over time; a small number never feel quite right; inflammation around the new joint in the first year occasionally requires the implant to be changed
Nerve or vessel injury, fracture around the implant, bleeding into the joint, kneecap dislocation (rare); nerve damage usually recovers over months
General risks of major surgery: breathing problems, heart attack or stroke, poor wound healing, allergic reactions to medicines, and very rarely death
alternatives: Exercise programmes, weight loss, walking aids, bracing
Steroid or hyaluronic acid injections
Partial knee replacement when only one compartment is worn, with a smaller incision and faster recovery
Osteotomy (realigning the bone) in younger patients with one-sided wear
Arthroscopy is not helpful for degenerative knees

cataract-surgery.name: Cataract surgery
cataract-surgery.what: The cloudy natural lens of the eye is broken up with ultrasound through a 2-3 mm incision at the edge of the cornea and sucked out, and a folded plastic lens is injected into the empty lens capsule where it unfolds. Done under drops or a local anaesthetic injection in 15-30 minutes, it is the commonest operation in the world. The technique is called phacoemulsification. The lens capsule, the thin bag that held the natural lens, is deliberately left in place to hold the implant, and the power of the implant is chosen from measurements of the eye taken beforehand. The person is awake and may be aware of light and movement but does not see the surgery itself; a steady flow of salty fluid over the eye during the operation is normal. It is regarded as one of the safest and most effective operations in medicine, and the great majority of people see better afterwards, although many still need glasses for reading or fine distance focus.
why: A cataract that blurs vision or causes glare enough to affect daily life, driving or work; there is no fixed level of vision at which surgery becomes necessary, and the decision rests on how much the cataract interferes with what the person needs to do
Rarely, to see the retina for treating diabetic eye disease, or to lower eye pressure in glaucoma
before: Eye measurements (biometry) to choose the lens power, aiming for distance or near focus; these are usually taken at a pre-assessment clinic, and the choice of focus is discussed because most people need glasses for whatever distance the implant is not set for
Drops to dilate the pupil on the day; anaesthetic drops or a small injection. Dilating drops blur vision for several hours, so driving to and from the appointment is not possible
No need to fast for local anaesthetic; regular medicines continued
steps: A tiny self-sealing incision is made at the edge of the cornea
A circular opening is torn in the front of the lens capsule (capsulorhexis), keeping the rest of the capsule intact to hold the new lens
An ultrasound probe emulsifies the lens nucleus, which is aspirated along with the softer cortex; the empty capsule is left behind
The folded intraocular lens is injected into the capsule and unfolds into place
The incision seals without stitches; antibiotic is placed in the eye. A stitch is occasionally needed if the wound does not self-seal
after: Home within an hour with a clear shield to wear at night for a week; someone else drives
Antibiotic and anti-inflammatory drops for about four weeks

Vision usually clears within days; new glasses after 4-6 weeks. Grittiness, a mild ache and redness are normal at first and fade over a day or two, though the eye can take a month or more to settle fully; colours often look brighter or bluer than before
Avoid rubbing the eye, swimming and heavy lifting for a couple of weeks, and keep soap and shampoo out of the eye
Sudden worsening of vision, increasing pain, or new flashes and shadows are reported to the eye clinic at once because they can signal infection, inflammation or retinal detachment
cataract-surgery.recovery: Most people see well within a few days and resume driving within one to two weeks once the eye meets the standard. The second eye is done weeks later. Discomfort is usually mild and short-lived, and the small incision heals on its own. Glasses are often still needed, almost always for reading and close work and sometimes to fine-tune distance vision. Months or years later the capsule behind the implant can thicken and cloud vision again; this is treated with a quick outpatient laser procedure and does not mean the cataract has returned.
risks: Posterior capsule opacification (cloudy membrane behind the lens) in up to a fifth over years, cleared with a quick laser
Infection inside the eye (endophthalmitis, about 1 in 1000), sight-threatening; sterile technique and antibiotics at the end of surgery reduce the risk

Tear of the capsule, retinal detachment, swelling of the retina, raised pressure. A tear in the back of the capsule is the main complication during surgery: it can let the gel inside the eye come forward, raises the later risk of retinal detachment and may mean the lens has to be placed differently
Bleeding inside the eye (rare) and inflammation after surgery that needs stronger treatment
Minor problems such as soreness, swelling or a mild surface infection are the commonest and settle with drops
A refractive surprise needing glasses or a lens exchange
alternatives: Stronger glasses and better lighting while the cataract is mild
No surgery, if vision is acceptable; cataracts do not damage the eye by waiting except when very advanced

angioplasty.name: Coronary angioplasty and stenting
angioplasty.what: A narrowed or blocked coronary artery is opened from inside. A fine wire is steered across the narrowing through a catheter from the wrist or groin, a balloon is inflated to crush the plaque against the wall, and a drug-coated metal mesh stent is expanded to hold the artery open. As primary PCI it is the emergency treatment for a heart attack; electively it relieves angina. It is a non-surgical procedure carried out by a cardiologist in a cardiac catheter laboratory, with X-ray screening and an iodine-based contrast agent to show the arteries. Only local anaesthetic and light sedation are needed, so the person is awake, and the puncture needs no stitches. Several balloon inflations, and sometimes more than one stent, may be needed to achieve a good result, and a straightforward case takes about half an hour to an hour. The stent stays in the artery permanently as a scaffold; antiplatelet medicines are then taken to stop a clot forming on it.
why: ST-elevation heart attack (STEMI): open the artery within 120 minutes of diagnosis. Reopening the blocked artery quickly limits the amount of heart muscle that dies
Non-ST-elevation heart attack and unstable angina, usually within days of admission, once the coronary anatomy has been mapped by angiography

Stable angina not controlled by medication, or with a large area of ischaemia on testing. Angina symptoms usually improve after stenting, although the procedure does not cure the underlying coronary artery disease
Where many arteries are badly narrowed, or the left main stem is involved, bypass surgery is usually advised instead of stents
before: ECG, troponin, kidney function, clotting; a loading dose of aspirin and a second antiplatelet. Kidney function matters because the contrast agent can reduce it, especially where the kidneys are already impaired
Any previous reaction to contrast dye, iodine or medicines is recorded, because an allergic reaction to the dye is a recognised though uncommon risk
An explanation of the procedure, its risks and the alternatives (medicines alone or bypass surgery), and written consent
Nil by mouth if elective; in an emergency straight to the catheter lab
Local anaesthetic to the wrist; mild sedation. A general anaesthetic is not used
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial (or femoral) artery under local anaesthetic and heparin is given to stop blood clotting on the equipment
Catheters are passed under X-ray screening to the origin of each coronary artery and contrast injected to map the narrowings; a brief warm flush is often felt as the dye goes in
A guidewire is steered across the lesion
A balloon is inflated for seconds to open the narrowing, with the ECG watched for ischaemia; a few inflations may be needed
A drug-eluting stent on a balloon is positioned and expanded to the artery's size; more than one stent is sometimes needed. A final angiogram confirms flow
The sheath is removed and the wrist compressed with a band, or the groin held under pressure or closed with a plug; no stitches are needed
after: Bed rest for a few hours (longer for femoral access); home the same or next day for elective cases, 2-3 days after a heart attack

Bruising and soreness at the puncture site and a tender chest are normal for a few days; mild chest discomfort in the first days is often the stent settling, but persistent or severe chest pain is checked urgently

Dual antiplatelet therapy for 6-12 months to stop clot forming on the stent, then aspirin for life. The second agent is clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor; stopping these medicines early without the cardiologist's advice is the main avoidable cause of stent thrombosis
Statin, beta blocker and ACE inhibitor as indicated; cardiac rehabilitation

Reasons to contact the unit or seek urgent help: bleeding from the wound that does not stop after firm pressure, increasing pain or swelling at the site, a high temperature, severe chest pain, or a limb that becomes cold, numb or swollen
angioplasty.recovery: Back to light activity within days and work in a week or two for elective procedures; after a heart attack, structured rehabilitation over 6-12 weeks. Heavy lifting and strenuous activity are avoided for about a week or until the wound has healed. After an emergency angioplasty for a heart attack it can take several weeks or months to recover fully, and the return to work and driving is guided by the cardiac rehabilitation team. Angina usually improves, but symptoms can return, more often than after bypass surgery, so the medicines and lifestyle changes that slow coronary disease remain essential.
risks: Bruising or bleeding at the puncture site, including a haematoma under the skin, is common and not usually serious; rarely the artery itself is damaged, which can affect the blood supply to the hand or leg
Contrast kidney injury and allergy; kidney function usually recovers but the risk is higher in people with diabetes or existing kidney disease

Heart attack, stroke or death during the procedure (well under 1% electively, higher in emergencies). A coronary artery can be damaged or blocked by the equipment; this is usually repaired during the procedure, but on rare occasions emergency bypass surgery is needed
Abnormal heart rhythms during the procedure (uncommon)

Stent thrombosis (rare, but serious if antiplatelets are stopped early); restenosis, where the treated segment narrows again within the stent over the following months and years, affects a minority and is reduced by drug-eluting stents and medicines
Emergency bypass surgery (rare)
Risks are greater when the procedure is done as an emergency or when complex blockages are treated
alternatives: Medication alone for stable angina (equally good for survival in many cases); angioplasty is reserved for angina that medicines do not control
Coronary artery bypass grafting for three-vessel or left main disease, especially with diabetes; after bypass, symptoms are less likely to return than after stenting
Thrombolysis (clot-busting drugs) when PCI cannot be delivered in time

coronary-bypass.name: Coronary artery bypass grafting
coronary-bypass.what: Open-heart surgery that routes blood around blocked coronary arteries using the patient's own vessels: the internal mammary artery from inside the chest wall is joined beyond the blockage in the left anterior descending artery, and lengths of leg vein or radial artery bridge from the aorta to the other vessels. Usually done on a heart-lung machine with the heart stopped. The operation takes several hours under general anaesthetic. It is usually performed through a full-length incision in the breastbone; in selected cases it can be done through smaller cuts with a camera, which is quicker to recover from but not suitable for everyone. Bypass relieves angina and breathlessness and lowers the risk of a heart attack in people with extensive disease, but it does not cure coronary artery disease: new blockages can form in the native arteries and in the grafts, so medicines and lifestyle changes continue for life.
why: Left main stem or three-vessel coronary disease, particularly with diabetes or a weak ventricle, where surgery improves survival compared with stents
Angina not controlled by medication where anatomy is unsuitable for stents
Failed or complicated angioplasty
Combined with valve surgery when both are needed
before: Coronary angiography and echocardiogram; carotid ultrasound; lung function, bloods, dental review. The risk of the operation is estimated from age, sex, diabetes, lung and kidney function and smoking, and discussed before consent
Stop clopidogrel a few days before; continue aspirin
General anaesthetic; arterial and central venous lines; urinary catheter
steps: The sternum is split lengthways and the internal mammary artery harvested from the chest wall while the vein is taken from the leg (or the radial artery from the arm)
Heparin is given and the heart-lung machine takes over circulation; the aorta is clamped and the heart arrested with cold potassium solution
Each graft is sewn with fine sutures to the coronary artery beyond its blockage; vein grafts are then joined to the aorta
The heart is restarted, the machine weaned off, and temporary pacing wires and chest drains placed
The sternum is closed with steel wires and the skin closed; the operation usually takes three to six hours
after: Intensive care overnight on a ventilator for a few hours, then the ward after a day or two; 5-8 days in hospital in total
Chest drains out in a day or two; pain from the sternum and leg wound; the heart rhythm is monitored continuously and temporary pacing used if needed
Aspirin, statin, beta blocker; medicines to prevent clots and irregular rhythm in the early days; cardiac rehabilitation from about six weeks
Tiredness, poor sleep and appetite, constipation, itching of the healing wounds and low mood or poor concentration are common in the first weeks and usually improve
Follow-up at about six to eight weeks, with an ECG or echocardiogram to check how the heart is working
coronary-bypass.recovery: Six to twelve weeks off work, no driving for four weeks, no heavy lifting for three months while the sternum knits; full benefit at about three months. Arterial grafts last decades; vein grafts about half are narrowed by ten years. Most people return to ordinary activities, including driving, work and sex, at about six weeks, later for heavy manual work. Recovery is quicker after minimally invasive bypass. Cardiac rehabilitation provides supervised exercise, education and psychological support, and most people notice a marked improvement in chest pain and breathlessness once they have recovered.
risks: Death (around 1-2% electively, higher in emergencies and with other illness, heart failure, lung or kidney disease)
Stroke (1-2%), heart attack, kidney injury (usually temporary, recovering over days or weeks)
Atrial fibrillation in a third (usually temporary and treated with a short course of medicine)
Wound infection, especially of the sternum in diabetes and obesity
Bleeding needing a return to theatre; memory and concentration changes for some months, which usually improve but can occasionally be permanent
Recurrence: the operation does not stop coronary disease, and new narrowings can develop in native arteries or grafts over the years
alternatives: Angioplasty and stents for suitable anatomy; symptoms are more likely to return than after bypass
Optimal medical therapy
Off-pump and minimally invasive bypass in selected cases

cardiac-catheterization.name: Cardiac catheterisation
cardiac-catheterization.what: Thin tubes are passed through an artery or vein to the heart to measure pressures and oxygen levels in its chambers, inject contrast into the coronary arteries and chambers, and, in electrophysiology studies, map the electrical circuits and burn or freeze the tissue causing an arrhythmia (ablation). The catheter is guided to the heart under X-ray screening from a blood vessel in the wrist, arm, groin or neck. Coronary angiography, the commonest form, shows whether and where the coronary arteries are narrowed or blocked, and if a suitable blockage is found angioplasty and stenting can be done in the same sitting. The person is awake, with local anaesthetic at the puncture site and a sedative if wanted, and can follow instructions during the test. A diagnostic study usually takes between half an hour and an hour; longer when treatment is added. It carries a slightly higher risk than non-invasive heart tests but is very safe in experienced hands.
why: Mapping coronary artery narrowing in angina or after a heart attack (before angioplasty or bypass); angiography remains the definitive test for deciding between medicines, stents and surgery
Assessing valve disease and heart failure by measuring pressures, including pulmonary hypertension, through right heart catheterisation
Diagnosing and ablating arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, SVT and atrial flutter
Closing holes in the heart, replacing valves through a catheter (TAVI), biopsy of heart muscle
before: Blood tests including kidney function and clotting; ECG; sometimes echo or CT. A stress test or heart imaging may be done first to see how well the heart is working and to plan the procedure

Fasting 4-6 hours; metformin and blood thinners managed. Allergies, especially any previous reaction to contrast dye or iodine, and any possibility of pregnancy are declared because X-rays and iodine contrast are used
The procedure, its risks and alternatives are explained and written consent is taken
Local anaesthetic to the wrist or groin, light sedation; awake throughout
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial artery (coronaries), femoral artery (left heart) or femoral vein (right heart, electrophysiology)
Catheters are advanced under X-ray screening to the coronary origins or heart chambers; some pressure or discomfort may be felt at the puncture site but not along the vessels

Contrast injections film the arteries from several angles as the X-ray machine moves around; a brief warm flush lasting a minute or two is normal as the dye goes in. Pressures and oxygen levels are recorded through the catheter
In electrophysiology, several electrode catheters map the rhythm; pacing provokes the arrhythmia and the culprit tissue is ablated
Sheaths are removed and the site compressed or closed with a plug; a pressure device or band is applied, and after wrist access the person can usually walk around straight away
after: Lie flat for 2-6 hours after femoral access; a wrist band for radial. Lying flat prevents bleeding from the groin artery and can cause some mild back discomfort
Home the same day for diagnostic studies; drink fluids to clear contrast. An overnight stay may be needed after treatment procedures or where other health problems make monitoring sensible
Results explained immediately with a plan for medication, stents or surgery

A bruise at the puncture site may last a few weeks; a lump under the skin (haematoma) should settle in a few days. Bleeding that does not stop, a cold or painful limb, chest pain or a fever are reported urgently
cardiac-catheterization.recovery: Normal activities within a day or two; avoid heavy lifting for a week. Ablation for atrial fibrillation is followed by anticoagulation for at least two months. Soreness and bruising at the wrist or groin are the commonest after-effects and fade over days to weeks. The team advises when regular medicines, driving and work can resume, which depends on the access site and on whether a stent or ablation was performed.
risks: Bruising, bleeding or a false aneurysm at the puncture site; rarely damage to the artery in the arm or groin that affects the blood supply to the limb

Contrast kidney injury or allergy; the dye can reduce kidney function, particularly in people with diabetes or existing kidney disease, so kidney function is checked beforehand and fluids encouraged afterwards
Stroke, heart attack, arrhythmia, perforation of the heart (all rare, well under 1%); low blood pressure, blood clots, infection and, with neck access, a collapsed lung are also rare
For ablation: damage to the heart's normal conduction needing a pacemaker (rare)
A small radiation dose, which matters most for children and for people who need repeated procedures
alternatives: CT coronary angiography for stable chest pain (no catheter, but no treatment possible)
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI for structure and function
Stress testing to look for ischaemia without imaging the arteries directly
Medication for arrhythmias instead of ablation

upper-endoscopy.name: Gastroscopy
upper-endoscopy.what: A thin flexible camera is passed through the mouth down the oesophagus, into the stomach and the first part of the small intestine, giving a direct view of the lining and allowing biopsies and treatment. It takes 5-15 minutes with throat spray or light sedation. Before the test a nurse reviews the medical history and medicines, explains the risks and takes written consent. The choice between throat spray alone and sedation is the person's: with throat spray they are fully awake and can leave soon afterwards, while sedation makes the test more comfortable but requires monitoring of breathing, pulse and blood pressure and an escort home. Gagging as the scope passes the back of the throat is normal and does not interfere with breathing. Air put into the stomach to open up the view causes bloating and belching and is sucked out at the end. Biopsies are painless because the lining of the gut has no pain sensation to the forceps. The examination can miss a small lesion, particularly if food remains in the stomach, which is why fasting beforehand matters.
why: Difficulty or pain on swallowing, persistent indigestion, especially over 55 or with weight loss
Vomiting blood or black stools (urgent, to find and treat the bleeding point)
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia
Diagnosing coeliac disease, H. pylori, Barrett oesophagus; surveillance of ulcers and Barrett
Treatment: stretching strictures, removing polyps, banding varices, placing feeding tubes and stents
before: Nothing to eat for 6 hours and clear fluids only until 2 hours before, so that the stomach is empty for a clear view and to lower the risk of inhaling stomach contents
Stop acid-suppressing tablets for two weeks if testing for H. pylori or ulcers is the aim

Blood thinners managed; a driver if sedated. All medicines are declared, including aspirin, anticoagulants, diabetes and blood pressure tablets, iron and anti-inflammatories, because some affect bleeding risk or need their timing adjusted around fasting
Dentures, loose teeth, crowns and bridgework are noted because the scope and mouthguard can occasionally damage them
steps: Lying on the left side with a mouthguard; throat spray numbs the gullet, or sedation is given through a cannula in the arm or hand
The scope is swallowed over the back of the tongue and advanced under direct vision; retching at this point is expected and passes
Air inflates the stomach for a clear view; the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum are inspected in turn
Biopsies are taken painlessly with forceps through the scope; polyps removed, bleeding treated with clips, injections or heat
The air is sucked out, the scope is withdrawn, and the whole procedure is recorded; pulse, oxygen and blood pressure are monitored throughout if sedation has been given
after: Sore throat and bloating for a day; mild stomach and throat discomfort passes within hours
Eat and drink once the throat spray has worn off (about an hour)
No driving, alcohol or important decisions for 24 hours after sedation; an adult escort is needed to go home
Biopsy results in one to two weeks, sometimes several weeks
Black, tarry stools, vomiting blood, severe or worsening abdominal or chest pain, or persistent bloating are reported to the emergency department because they may indicate bleeding or a perforation
upper-endoscopy.recovery: Normal activities the same day (next day after sedation). The immediate findings are usually explained before discharge; biopsy results decide treatment for coeliac disease, H. pylori, Barrett oesophagus or suspected cancer and are given at a follow-up appointment or by letter.
risks: Sore throat, bloating
Bleeding after biopsy or polyp removal (small), higher in people taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs

Perforation of the oesophagus or stomach (about 1 in 3000, higher with stretching); a tear may need admission or surgery, and the risk is higher after therapeutic procedures such as dilatation than after a diagnostic test
Reaction to sedation, which can slow breathing, lower blood pressure or disturb heart rhythm, more so in older people and those with other illnesses; chest infection from aspiration (rare)
Damage to teeth, crowns or bridgework (slight risk)
A small lesion may be missed, particularly if the stomach has not emptied
alternatives: Barium swallow or CT (no biopsies)
Capsule endoscopy for the small bowel
A trial of acid suppression in younger patients without alarm features
Non-invasive tests for H. pylori (breath or stool test) when no view of the lining is needed

colonoscopy.name: Colonoscopy
colonoscopy.what: A flexible camera is passed through the anus around the whole large intestine to the caecum and often into the last part of the small intestine. Polyps found on the way are removed, which prevents them growing into cancer; this is why screening colonoscopy reduces bowel cancer deaths. The value of the test depends almost entirely on the bowel being completely empty: residual stool hides the lining, lowers the chance of reaching the caecum and of detecting adenomas, and can mean the examination has to be repeated. Inadequate preparation is common, and is more likely in men, in people with diabetes and after previous abdominal surgery, so the preparation instructions are followed closely. Most other medicines, including aspirin, are usually continued, while iron tablets are stopped beforehand because they coat the bowel wall. The test is done with sedation and a painkiller, or with gas and air, and the whole examination is recorded with photographs of landmarks and any abnormality.
why: A positive stool screening test (FIT) or bleeding from the bowel
Change in bowel habit, unexplained weight loss or iron-deficiency anaemia
Diagnosing and monitoring inflammatory bowel disease, with biopsies to confirm the type and extent of inflammation
Surveillance after polyps or bowel cancer, and in high-risk families
Removing polyps, stopping bleeding, dilating strictures, decompressing a twisted bowel
before: Low-fibre diet for a few days, then strong laxative bowel preparation the day before, drinking litres of clear fluid until the output runs clear; red or purple drinks are avoided because the dye can look like blood
Iron tablets stopped a week before; blood thinners and diabetes medicines adjusted. Aspirin is usually continued; anticoagulants may need to be paused if polyp removal is likely

The laxatives cause nausea, cramps, bloating and frequent watery stools; drinking plenty of clear fluid prevents dehydration and salt imbalance, which matter most in the frail and in people with kidney or heart disease
Sedation and painkiller through a cannula, or gas and air; a driver is arranged if sedation is used
steps: Lying on the left side; the lubricated scope is inserted and advanced with carbon dioxide inflating the bowel
The scope is steered around the sigmoid, descending, transverse and ascending colon to the caecum, changing position or with abdominal pressure to straighten loops
The lining is inspected carefully on the slow withdrawal (at least six minutes)
Polyps are snared with a wire loop and cut with diathermy, or removed cold if small; larger lesions lifted and resected in pieces
Biopsies are taken from any abnormal or inflamed areas; all specimens go to histology
Blood pressure, pulse and oxygen are monitored throughout when sedation is used, because sedatives can lower blood pressure and breathing
after: Wind and cramps for a few hours as gas passes
Eat and drink normally; a little blood after polypectomy is expected
No driving for 24 hours after sedation
Histology in one to two weeks decides surveillance intervals
Severe abdominal pain, heavy rectal bleeding, fever, or dizziness and reduced urine output suggesting dehydration are reported urgently; bleeding after polyp removal can be delayed by up to a week
colonoscopy.recovery: Normal activities the next day. The findings are usually explained before discharge: a normal examination with good preparation is reassuring, removed polyps are classified by histology to set the interval to the next check, and biopsies of inflamed areas guide treatment of inflammatory bowel disease. If the preparation was poor or the caecum could not be reached, a repeat colonoscopy or CT colonography is arranged.
risks: Bleeding after polyp removal (about 1 in 100 for large polyps, sometimes delayed by a week); the risk is higher on anticoagulants
Perforation (about 1 in 1000-2000), more after resection of large polyps; may need surgery
Missed lesions (some per cent, especially with poor preparation); poor preparation also lowers the chance of completing the examination
Reaction to sedation, including low blood pressure or oxygen; dehydration and salt imbalance from bowel preparation in the frail
Side effects of the preparation itself: nausea, vomiting, bloating, cramps, headache and anal soreness, usually mild; occasionally the procedure has to be abandoned because of them
alternatives: CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy): no sedation, but no biopsies and needs colonoscopy if abnormal
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: examines only the left colon with an enema
Capsule colonoscopy in selected cases

bronchoscopy.name: Bronchoscopy
bronchoscopy.what: A thin flexible scope is passed through the nose or mouth, between the vocal cords and down the trachea into the bronchi of each lung, to inspect the airways, wash out or brush cells, and take biopsies. Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) adds an ultrasound probe on the scope tip so lymph nodes beside the airways can be sampled with a needle through the wall.
why: A lung mass or shadow on CT, to diagnose and stage lung cancer
Coughing up blood
Persistent infection or collapse of a lung segment; sampling in immunosuppressed patients
Removing inhaled foreign bodies and mucus plugs; placing airway stents
Diagnosing sarcoidosis, tuberculosis and interstitial lung disease (cryobiopsy)
before: CT of the chest; clotting and blood count; spirometry and oxygen level
Fasting 4-6 hours; blood thinners managed
Local anaesthetic spray to the nose and throat plus sedation; oxygen through the nose; monitoring throughout
steps: The scope passes through the nostril, over the back of the tongue, and lidocaine is sprayed onto the vocal cords before passing between them
The trachea and the bronchial tree of both lungs are inspected to segmental level
Saline washings (lavage) are instilled and suctioned for microbiology and cytology; brushings scrape cells from a lesion
Forceps biopsies are taken from visible tumours; transbronchial biopsies from lung tissue beyond view, sometimes under X-ray guidance
With EBUS, a needle passes through the airway wall into lymph nodes under ultrasound view
after: Nothing to eat or drink until the throat numbness wears off (1-2 hours)
Mild cough, sore throat, a little blood-streaked sputum for a day
A chest X-ray if transbronchial biopsies were taken, to check for a collapsed lung
No driving for 24 hours; results in a week or two
risks: Low oxygen and breathlessness during the procedure
Bleeding, usually minor
Pneumothorax (collapsed lung) after transbronchial biopsy (a few per cent)
Fever, infection, arrhythmia, laryngospasm (rare)
alternatives: CT-guided needle biopsy through the chest wall for peripheral lesions
Sputum cytology and blood tests
Surgical biopsy (mediastinoscopy, VATS)

dialysis.name: Dialysis
dialysis.what: Artificial replacement of the kidneys' filtering work when they have failed. In haemodialysis, blood is pumped from a vascular access through a filter where waste and excess water pass across a membrane into dialysis fluid, then returned, usually for four hours three times a week. In peritoneal dialysis, fluid is run into the abdomen through a permanent catheter and the peritoneum itself acts as the membrane, exchanged several times a day or overnight by a machine. In both forms waste solutes move from blood into the dialysis fluid by diffusion down a concentration gradient, and water is drawn off by osmosis or pressure, so the composition of the fluid determines what is removed. Dialysis replaces only part of what healthy kidneys do: it clears waste and fluid but not the hormone functions, so anaemia, bone disease and blood pressure still need separate treatment. Both types can be done at home; peritoneal dialysis is needle-free, controls fluid more steadily and allows a less restricted diet, while haemodialysis in a unit is supervised by staff. The choice depends on medical factors, lifestyle and preference, and people can switch between them.
why: End-stage kidney disease (eGFR under about 10, or symptoms of uraemia, fluid overload or high potassium that medication cannot control)
Acute kidney injury with life-threatening potassium, acidosis, fluid overload or toxins, as a temporary measure until the kidneys recover
Some poisonings (lithium, methanol, aspirin overdose)
before: Months of planning in advanced kidney disease: education, choosing the type, vaccination against hepatitis B

Creating access: an arteriovenous fistula joining the radial artery and cephalic vein at the wrist (or a graft), which needs 6-12 weeks to mature; or a tunnelled catheter in the internal jugular vein for urgent starts. The fistula operation is done under local anaesthetic and takes about an hour; a fistula is preferred because catheters carry a much higher rate of bloodstream infection
For peritoneal dialysis, a catheter placed into the abdomen two weeks before use, with training in the sterile technique for exchanges
Unplanned 'urgent-start' dialysis through a catheter has more early complications than a planned start through mature access, which is why preparation begins well before the kidneys fail
steps: Haemodialysis: two needles in the fistula (or the catheter connected); blood flows at 300-400 mL/min through the dialyser; heparin prevents clotting; the machine removes a set volume of fluid; weight, blood pressure and bloods are monitored

Peritoneal dialysis: 2 litres of warmed glucose-based fluid drains into the abdomen, dwells for hours while waste and water diffuse across the peritoneum, then drains out; repeated 4 times a day (CAPD) or by a cycler overnight (APD). Each exchange takes about half an hour to forty minutes
Diet restricts potassium, phosphate, salt and fluid; phosphate binders, erythropoietin and vitamin D replace kidney functions dialysis cannot
after: Tiredness and cramps after haemodialysis sessions are common; cramps are felt mainly in the lower legs and are thought to reflect the fluid removed during the session
Regular monthly bloods, adequacy checks and fistula care
Itchy skin, poor sleep, bone and joint pain, dry mouth, low mood or anxiety and loss of libido are common long-term problems that the team can help with
Assessment for a kidney transplant, which offers the best survival and quality of life
dialysis.recovery: Dialysis is ongoing rather than a one-off procedure; many people continue work and travel, with peritoneal or home haemodialysis giving more flexibility. Fatigue is the commonest long-term complaint with either type. Peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis is treated with antibiotics and most episodes settle, but severe or repeated infection may mean switching to haemodialysis. Survival on the two types is similar overall, so the decision rests on suitability and on what fits the person's life.
risks: Low blood pressure, cramps, nausea and dizziness during haemodialysis sessions, caused by the fall in fluid volume as water is removed
Access problems: fistula clotting or narrowing, catheter infection and bloodstream infection; people on haemodialysis are at increased risk of sepsis

Peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis (about one episode every 2-3 years), usually from skin bacteria entering at the catheter; warning signs are abdominal pain, fever, nausea, chills and cloudy drained fluid. Mechanical problems such as fluid leaks around the catheter and poor drainage also occur
Protein loss into peritoneal fluid causing low energy and malnutrition, and weight gain from the glucose in the fluid
Long term: cardiovascular disease, bone disease, amyloid, anaemia; life expectancy is reduced compared with transplantation
alternatives: Kidney transplantation (living or deceased donor), pre-emptively where possible
Conservative kidney management: symptom control without dialysis, chosen by some frail or elderly patients

blood-transfusion.name: Blood transfusion
blood-transfusion.what: Donated blood components given into a vein: red cells for anaemia and blood loss, platelets for low counts with bleeding, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate for clotting factor deficiency. Each unit is matched to the recipient's ABO and RhD blood groups and screened for antibodies, and identity is checked at every step. Transfusion treats a shortage of a particular blood component rather than 'blood' as a whole, so only the component that is lacking is given. It takes place in hospital, through a cannula in a vein, and the person is monitored throughout. All donated blood is tested for serious infections such as hepatitis and HIV before it is released, and the recipient's own sample is tested so that compatible units are selected (cross-matching); this is done before every transfusion except in a life-threatening emergency, when group O blood may be given first.
why: Major bleeding from trauma, surgery, the gut or childbirth

Symptomatic anaemia that cannot wait for iron or other treatment; haemoglobin below about 70 g/L in stable patients (80 in heart disease). A transfusion is not given simply to correct a number: the decision weighs symptoms, the cause of the anaemia and whether a slower treatment would work
Bone marrow failure and chemotherapy, where cancers or their treatment stop the marrow making enough red cells or platelets
Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia (regular transfusions), which carry the particular long-term problem of iron overload
Reversing clotting problems before surgery or in massive haemorrhage, using platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate rather than red cells
before: A group-and-save or crossmatch sample, labelled at the bedside from a wristband check. The laboratory tests the sample against donor units so that the blood given is a good match; most serious reactions come from mismatched blood, and cross-matching is designed to catch this

Consent, explaining benefits, risks and alternatives; baseline temperature, pulse and blood pressure. Previous transfusions, pregnancies and any earlier reaction are recorded because they can leave antibodies that make matching harder
A cannula in a forearm vein
steps: Two staff check the unit against the patient's identity and the compatibility label; most incompatible transfusions result from a clerical or identification error rather than a laboratory failure, which is why the check is repeated at the bedside
Red cells run over 1.5-3 hours (faster in emergencies); platelets over 30 minutes; plasma over 30-60 minutes
Observations are repeated at 15 minutes and at the end of each unit

Any fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, back or flank pain, dark urine, flushing or dizziness stops the transfusion immediately for assessment; a mild temperature or rash may be treated with paracetamol and by slowing the rate once a serious reaction has been excluded
Haemoglobin is rechecked after; each unit of red cells raises it by about 10 g/L
after: Most people feel better within hours if anaemia was symptomatic
A sore arm or bruise at the needle site for a few days is common

Delayed reactions (jaundice, falling haemoglobin) can occur a week or so later, when antibodies formed against the donor cells destroy them; new symptoms in the days after a transfusion are reported to the care team
Women of childbearing age receive RhD-matched and K-negative blood to protect future pregnancies
blood-transfusion.recovery: Usually a day-case or in-patient treatment with no recovery period of its own. The benefit depends on the reason for transfusion: symptoms of anaemia such as breathlessness and tiredness often ease within hours, while the underlying cause still needs treatment so that the haemoglobin does not simply fall again. People who need transfusions regularly are monitored for iron overload and for antibodies that can make future matching more difficult.
risks: Mild fever or hives (about 1 in 100); itching, rash, fever and headache are the commonest reactions and are usually mild

Fluid overload in the elderly and heart failure (the commonest serious harm), prevented by slow rates and diuretics; it is most likely when a large volume is given quickly and can cause fluid on the lungs

Acute haemolytic reaction from a wrong-blood error (rare but can be fatal), why identity checks are strict: the immune system destroys the donated cells, which can cause kidney failure, shock and clotting problems
Severe allergic reactions with breathing difficulty, chest or back pain and a fast pulse (rare)
Transfusion-related acute lung injury, bacterial contamination of platelets, and iron overload with repeated transfusion, which can damage the liver and heart
Alloimmunisation: forming antibodies against donor red cells, which can cause delayed reactions and complicate future transfusions and pregnancies
Infection transmission is extremely rare with modern screening (HIV about 1 in several million)
alternatives: Iron (oral or intravenous), B12, folate and erythropoietin for anaemia with time to respond
Tranexamic acid and cell salvage in surgery to reduce the need
Patient blood management: correcting anaemia before planned surgery
Giving only the component that is lacking (platelets or plasma rather than red cells) so that whole-blood transfusion is rarely needed
blood-transfusion.summary: Donated red cells, platelets or plasma are given into a vein, matched to the recipient's blood group and checked at every step, to treat anaemia, blood loss or clotting failure.

urinary-catheterization.name: Urinary catheterisation
urinary-catheterization.what: A soft tube passed along the urethra into the bladder to drain urine, held in place by a small balloon inflated inside the bladder. Used for hours during surgery, days on a ward, or long term when the bladder cannot empty. A suprapubic catheter enters through the lower abdominal wall instead; intermittent catheterisation passes a tube several times a day and removes it each time. Intermittent catheters are usually single-use and are passed either at set times or when the bladder feels full; they avoid the continuous presence of a foreign body in the bladder and so carry fewer long-term problems. An indwelling catheter drains into a leg bag or, with a valve, is emptied directly into the toilet. A suprapubic catheter is chosen when the urethra is damaged or blocked, or when intermittent catheterisation is not possible. Catheter-associated urinary infection is the commonest healthcare-associated infection, and the single most effective way to prevent it is to avoid catheters that are not needed and to remove them as soon as they are. Most people with a long-term catheter can live a relatively normal life, including work, exercise, swimming, travel and sex, with guidance from a continence nurse.
why: Acute urinary retention (usually from an enlarged prostate) or chronic retention with kidney damage
Measuring urine output hour by hour in critical illness and major surgery
Neurological bladder problems (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis), often by self-catheterisation
Bladder irrigation after prostate or bladder surgery, or with clots
Incontinence with skin breakdown when other measures fail (last resort)
before: Explanation and consent; checking for latex allergy and previous difficult catheters. A history of prostate enlargement, urethral stricture or earlier failed attempts predicts a difficult insertion, when a urologist or specialist nurse is involved early rather than after repeated tries
Sterile technique: hand hygiene, gloves, cleaning the urethral opening
Anaesthetic lubricant gel instilled into the urethra and left for a few minutes
The smallest catheter that will drain adequately is chosen, because larger tubes put more pressure on the lining of the urethra
steps: The catheter (usually 12-16 Fr) is advanced gently along the urethra; in women the short urethra opens just above the vagina, and in men the penis is held upright to straighten the first bend, then lowered to pass the prostate

Urine flows once the tip is in the bladder; the catheter is advanced further before the balloon is inflated with 10 mL of sterile water. The balloon is never inflated until urine has been seen, because inflating it in the urethra causes serious injury
It is drawn back until the balloon rests at the bladder neck and connected to a drainage bag or valve
The volume drained is recorded; very large volumes are drained in stages if chronic retention is suspected
The catheter is secured to the thigh to prevent traction; the insertion, catheter size and planned review date are documented, often in a catheter passport the person keeps
If the catheter will not pass, force is not used: repeated failed attempts cause urethral trauma, false passages, bleeding and later strictures, so a different technique or specialist help is sought
after: Daily cleaning of the meatus, keeping the bag below bladder level and changing bags on schedule
Removal (trial without catheter) as soon as it is no longer needed, usually within days; every day in place adds to the infection risk
Long-term catheters are changed every 4-12 weeks; bacteria in the urine are expected and not treated unless there are symptoms

Leaking around the catheter (bypassing) can result from bladder spasms or straining at stool, and can also be the first sign that the catheter is blocked; severe or persistent spasm, blockage or no drainage is reported promptly to the community nurse
Fever, rigors, loin pain, confusion or feeling generally unwell with a catheter in place suggest infection spreading to the kidneys or blood and need same-day assessment
urinary-catheterization.recovery: Slight stinging on first passing urine after removal is normal; a failed trial without catheter leads to re-catheterisation and urology review. People discharged with a catheter are taught bag changes, hygiene and what to do about leakage or blockage, and are given a date for removal or change. Adjusting to a long-term catheter takes time, and discomfort, urgency, bladder spasm and blood in the urine are commonly reported in the first weeks.
risks: Urinary tract infection, rising with each day in place, and catheter-related sepsis; most bacteria in the urine cause no symptoms, but a proportion progress to infection needing treatment
Urethral trauma, bleeding and false passage, especially in men with strictures or enlarged prostates, and after repeated insertion attempts
Blockage by debris or clots; bypassing; bladder spasm; pain and discomfort, and in men painful erections
Rarely, misplacement of the catheter or balloon in the urethra or a ureter, or injury to the bladder wall, more likely in people with reduced sensation from neurological disease
Long term: strictures, stones, bladder cancer risk after many years; pressure damage to the urethra and penis from a poorly secured catheter; effects on sexual function and self-image
alternatives: Bladder scan and watchful measures for mild retention
Alpha-blocker tablets before a trial without catheter in prostatic retention
Intermittent self-catheterisation or suprapubic catheter for long-term needs; sex is usually easier with these than with an indwelling urethral catheter
Sheath (condom) drainage or pads for incontinence

joint-aspiration.name: Joint aspiration and injection
joint-aspiration.what: A needle is passed into a swollen joint to draw off fluid for analysis and to relieve pressure, often followed by an injection of corticosteroid and local anaesthetic through the same needle to settle inflammation. The knee is the commonest site; the shoulder, wrist, elbow, ankle and hip (with ultrasound guidance) are also done. Analysis of the fluid is the definitive way to diagnose infection in a joint and crystal arthritis, and helps sort out other causes of arthritis. The appearance of the fluid is itself informative: increasing inflammation goes with more fluid, lower viscosity, greater cloudiness and a higher cell count dominated by neutrophils, while frank blood points to injury or a bleeding disorder. Strict sterile technique protects the joint from infection and also keeps the sample uncontaminated so the laboratory results can be trusted. Ultrasound guidance improves the chance of obtaining fluid and reduces complications, particularly in small or deep joints. The only absolute reason not to aspirate is infected skin over the entry point; a suspected septic joint is aspirated even in someone who is unwell, because the fluid result changes management.
why: A hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis must be ruled out (the fluid goes for urgent microscopy and culture); Gram stain is prioritised if only a little fluid is obtained, and culture confirms the diagnosis because the stain misses many early infections
Diagnosing gout and pseudogout by finding crystals under polarised light
Relieving a tense, painful effusion after injury or in osteoarthritis, which also restores movement
Joint pain or swelling of unknown cause, where the fluid cell count and composition separate inflammatory from non-inflammatory arthritis
Steroid injection for osteoarthritis flares, rheumatoid arthritis, frozen shoulder, bursitis and tendon sheath inflammation
before: Explain and consent; check for anticoagulants (not a contraindication for most joints), skin infection over the site, and allergy. Infected skin (cellulitis) over the planned entry point is the one absolute contraindication; bacteria in the bloodstream is a relative concern because the needle could seed the joint
Position the joint: the knee slightly bent over a roll; the landmark chosen beside the patella
Skin cleaned with antiseptic; sterile gloves; local anaesthetic to the skin optional; ultrasound used for deep joints or when landmarks are uncertain
steps: A needle (18-21 gauge) on a syringe is advanced through the skin into the joint space using landmarks or ultrasound, with a giving-way as it enters
Fluid is aspirated: its colour and clarity noted (clear yellow, cloudy, bloody, pus)
Samples are sent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and crystal examination; glucose, protein and lactate may be measured as supporting evidence of infection
If indicated, the syringe is swapped and steroid (for example 40 mg methylprednisolone or triamcinolone) with lidocaine is injected
The needle is withdrawn and a dressing applied; the fluid volume is recorded
after: Rest the joint for 24-48 hours after a steroid injection; ice for discomfort; simple painkillers may be needed for the first day or two

Watch for a flare of pain in the first day (crystal reaction to the steroid) and for redness, fever or increasing pain suggesting infection; a marked increase in pain with swelling, restricted movement, fever and feeling unwell needs same-day assessment
Diabetics: blood glucose may rise for a few days
Results: Gram stain and cell count are available within hours and guide whether antibiotics are started; culture takes days; if the fluid is inconclusive a synovial biopsy may be considered
joint-aspiration.recovery: Relief from an aspiration is immediate; steroid benefit builds over a few days and lasts weeks to months. The injection acts quickly and the effect can last for months, but it treats inflammation rather than the underlying cause, so the diagnosis still needs to be established. Repeated injections into the same joint are limited because of concern about cartilage and surrounding tissue.
risks: Introducing infection into the joint (about 1 in 10,000 with sterile technique)
Bleeding into the joint, especially on anticoagulants
Post-injection flare, skin thinning or pale patch at the site, facial flushing; thinning of the fat under the skin can leave a small dimple months later
Steroid deposits visible on later X-rays, which are harmless
Cartilage damage with repeated steroid injections (limit to 3-4 a year)
alternatives: Oral anti-inflammatories and rest
Physiotherapy and bracing
Ultrasound-guided injection for deep or difficult joints
Arthroscopy for mechanical problems, or synovial biopsy when fluid analysis is inconclusive

joint-aspiration.summary: A needle drawn into a swollen joint removes fluid for analysis and relief of pressure, and may be followed by a corticosteroid injection; it is the definitive way to diagnose septic and crystal arthritis.

caesarean-section.name: Caesarean section
caesarean-section.what: Birth of a baby through a cut in the lower abdomen and in the lower segment of the uterus, usually under a spinal or epidural anaesthetic so that the person is awake and a birth partner can be present. The operation is the same for trans men and non-binary people who give birth. It is one of the commonest operations carried out in the UK and accounts for a substantial proportion of births. A planned (elective) caesarean is booked in advance, normally after 39 weeks; an unplanned one is done during pregnancy or labour, and its urgency ranges from an immediate threat to the life of the woman or the baby, when the baby is delivered within minutes, to a decision that can wait for the next available theatre. Urgency is graded in four categories, from an immediate threat to life through to a caesarean timed to suit the woman and the team.
why: The baby lies breech or across the uterus, or turning the baby by external cephalic version has not worked or is not suitable
The placenta covers or lies close to the cervix (placenta praevia), or is abnormally attached to the scar of an earlier caesarean
A twin or higher-order pregnancy where the first baby is not head-down, or where labour is not thought to be safe
Concern about the baby during labour, such as an abnormal heart rate pattern, bleeding from the placenta or a cord prolapse
Labour that does not progress, or a baby in a position that cannot pass through the pelvis
Maternal conditions such as severe pre-eclampsia, and some infections that could be passed to the baby during a vaginal birth

A previous caesarean, where a planned repeat operation is chosen rather than a vaginal birth after caesarean, or a request for a caesarean birth after the risks and benefits of both routes have been discussed
before: A discussion of the reasons, the risks of caesarean and of vaginal birth, and what the recovery involves, with written consent
A blood count and a group and save sample, with anaemia treated beforehand where there is time; an ultrasound to confirm the position of the baby and the placenta
Fasting and a medicine to reduce stomach acid, because of the small risk of acid entering the lungs under anaesthetic
A spinal or epidural anaesthetic in most cases, with a general anaesthetic kept for the most urgent operations or when a regional block is not possible
Antibiotics before the skin is cut, clot-prevention stockings, and a catheter passed once the anaesthetic is working
steps: The anaesthetic is tested to make sure the abdomen is numb, the skin is cleaned and draped, and a screen is placed so that the birth can still be watched if the parents wish

A transverse incision is made a little above the pubic bone and deepened to the rectus sheath, which is opened and lifted; the rectus muscles are separated in the midline, keeping clear of the inferior epigastric vessels at their outer edges, and the peritoneum is opened
The fold of peritoneum over the lower segment of the uterus is incised and the bladder is gently pushed downwards out of the way

A small transverse cut is made in the lower segment and opened out with the fingers; the membranes are ruptured and the head, or the breech, is delivered with a hand and pressure on the fundus, occasionally helped by forceps or a vacuum cup

The cord is clamped, after a short delay when the baby is well, and a drug that contracts the uterus is given so that the placenta separates and is delivered by controlled traction on the cord; the cavity is checked to be empty
The uterine incision is closed, normally in two layers, bleeding is checked, swabs and instruments are counted, the sheath is closed and the skin is closed with a suture or clips

A vertical (classical) incision in the uterus is used only occasionally, for example at very early gestations or when the lower segment cannot be reached safely, and it changes the advice about future births
after: Skin-to-skin contact and the first feed usually start in theatre or in recovery, with help to find a position that keeps the baby off the wound

The catheter comes out once the anaesthetic has worn off and walking, eating and drinking start early; regular pain relief is given and clot-prevention injections continue for a period after discharge
The dressing is removed after a day or two and the wound is kept clean and dry; clips or non-absorbable stitches are taken out by a midwife

Vaginal bleeding (lochia) continues for a few weeks, as it does after any birth; bleeding that becomes heavy again or passes large clots, offensive-smelling discharge, fever, a severe headache with visual disturbance, calf pain or breathlessness are reported to the maternity unit or NHS 111 straight away
caesarean-section.recovery: Most people stay in hospital for one to two days and feel a little stronger each week over about six weeks. Driving restarts when an emergency stop can be done comfortably, and lifting anything heavier than the baby is avoided at first. The scar sits low and fades over about a year; numbness around it is common and usually improves.
risks: Infection of the wound, the lining of the uterus or the urine, and heavier bleeding than at a vaginal birth, occasionally needing a transfusion
Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), which is why clot prevention and early walking matter
Injury to the bladder, and less often to the ureter or bowel, which is more likely when there are adhesions from previous surgery
A small cut to the baby's skin at the time of delivery, and a greater chance of short-lived breathing difficulty in the baby, which is less common after 39 weeks
Effects on later pregnancies: a placenta lying low or growing into the scar, and a small risk of the scar giving way in a future labour
A longer recovery than an uncomplicated vaginal birth, and adhesions that can make later abdominal surgery harder
Uncommonly, further surgery is needed, including removal of the uterus (hysterectomy) if bleeding cannot be controlled by other means
alternatives: Vaginal birth, including a planned vaginal birth after a previous caesarean once the risks have been discussed
Induction of labour where the concern is about continuing the pregnancy rather than about labour itself
An assisted vaginal birth with forceps or a vacuum cup when the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low enough
External cephalic version to turn a breech baby head-down before labour

chest-masculinisation.name: Chest masculinisation (top surgery)
chest-masculinisation.what: Removal of most of the breast tissue and excess skin, with resizing and repositioning of the nipples, to give a flat chest with a male contour; a common gender-affirming operation for trans men and non-binary people assigned female at birth. It is not the same as a mastectomy for cancer: a thin layer of tissue is deliberately left for an even contour, so a small amount of breast tissue remains. The complementary operation for trans women, breast augmentation, places implants under or over the pectoralis major once oestrogen-driven breast growth has settled. Gender incongruence is not a mental illness: the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health, and chest surgery is one option that some, not all, trans people choose.
why: Gender incongruence in trans men and non-binary people who want a flat, masculine chest, after assessment under the WPATH Standards of Care; hormone therapy is not a prerequisite
Relief from long-term chest binding, which can cause skin damage, rib and back pain and restricted breathing
Breast augmentation for trans women whose breast growth on oestrogen is less than they want, usually judged once growth has largely stopped, which commonly takes two to three years of hormone therapy
before: Assessment by a gender identity service following the WPATH Standards of Care: a settled decision and capacity to consent; testosterone is not required, although many people are taking it

Stopping smoking, which impairs nipple graft and wound healing, and weight optimised; breast imaging (mammography or ultrasound) beforehand where the surgeon's protocol or age, a family history of breast cancer or a lump warrants it
Choice of technique from chest size and skin elasticity: periareolar or keyhole for small chests with elastic skin, double incision with free nipple grafts for larger chests or loose skin
Markings made standing; fasting; general anaesthetic; antibiotics at induction and clot-prevention measures
steps: Double incision: a curved incision along the lower border of each breast, following the line of the pectoral fold; the breast tissue and excess skin are lifted off the fascia of pectoralis major and removed, leaving a thin even layer of fat for a natural contour
Liposuction blends the edges and the axillary tail into the chest wall and armpit

Each nipple-areola complex is removed, trimmed to a smaller male size and replaced as a free graft lower and further out on the chest, held with a tie-over dressing; the graft has no blood or nerve supply of its own and must take from the bed beneath
Keyhole: a short incision at the lower border of the areola through which the tissue is removed, with no skin excised, for a small chest with elastic skin
Periareolar: an incision around the whole areola, with a ring of skin removed and a purse-string suture tightening the skin around it; in both the nipple stays on its own blood and nerve supply
Drains are placed, the incisions closed in layers and a compression binder or dressing applied
Breast augmentation (trans women): through an incision under the breast, around the areola or in the armpit, a pocket is made under or over pectoralis major and a silicone or saline implant placed
after: Home the same day or after one night; drains removed within days; nipple graft dressings left undisturbed for about a week
A compression binder worn for about 4-6 weeks; no lifting, reaching overhead or vigorous exercise during that time

Nipple grafts look dark and crusted at first and take weeks to settle; sensation in grafted nipples is largely lost and does not fully return, whereas periareolar and keyhole techniques, which keep the nipple on its own nerve supply, more often preserve some sensation, although it may still be reduced
Scar care (massage, sun protection, silicone tape as advised); a lump or change in the remaining tissue still needs assessment, and screening advice afterwards is individual
The tissue removed is sent for examination under the microscope; an unexpected abnormality is uncommon but is followed up in the usual way
chest-masculinisation.recovery: Desk work within 1-2 weeks and full activity by about 6 weeks; swelling settles over months and the scars fade and mature over about a year. Chest wall sensation is altered for months, and grafted nipples usually stay numb.
risks: Haematoma (blood collecting under the skin, the main early complication) and seroma (fluid), sometimes needing drainage
Infection and delayed wound healing, more likely in smokers
Partial or complete loss of a nipple graft, loss of pigment, or a nipple of unexpected shape or position
Loss of nipple sensation (expected with free grafts), scarring and keloid, asymmetry and bunching of skin at the ends of the scars ('dog ears'), with revision surgery sometimes needed

Residual breast tissue: chest surgery lowers but does not remove the possibility of breast cancer, so any new lump, skin change or nipple change still needs assessment, and screening advice after surgery is decided individually
alternatives: Chest binding with a purpose-made binder, with limits on hours, regular breaks and never while sleeping, to reduce skin, rib and breathing problems
Hormone therapy and social transition without surgery; not everyone wants surgery
Liposuction alone for small chests made up mainly of fat
For trans women: prosthetic breast forms, fat transfer, or continuing oestrogen, since breast growth continues for two to three years
